pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 15: Growing: pea (8 cm). Problems: Yusuf.*

Yusuf has been following me for three days, which he does with the subtle grace of a marching band, stomping his small rubber boots on the concrete as if he is trying to knock on a door that is already open. I did not hear him until he squeezed through the gap in the fence, which is tight even for me, and let out a shout that startled a sparrow off the pear tree.

"THERE IS A TORTOISE," he announced, his voice cracking on the word like a dry twig snapping underfoot.

I covered my mouth, but it was too late. Gherkin stopped chewing his lettuce and turned his head, very slowly, toward the noise. Yusuf was grinning, his missing front teeth making his smile look like a stage with no actors on it, and he did not stop shouting. He just started shouting louder, about the green leaves and the rusty tin and the fact that a bird was looking at him with judgment.

I looked at Gherkin. Gherkin looked at Yusuf.

"Mm," Gherkin said.

"Can I keep it?" Yusuf asked.

"No," I said.

"I can keep the secret," Yusuf promised, which was not what he was asked.
pages.image: A small boy with missing front teeth squeezes through a chain-link fence gap, shouting excitedly at a mossy tortoise on a stone path; a thin girl with round glasses covers her mouth in the background, looking worried.

pages.text:
Yusuf had one hundred questions, and he fired them off like a machine gun loaded with curiosity. "How old are you? Do you eat lettuce? Do you like lettuce? Is that lettuce? Is that a hat? Can I touch the hat? Why is it green? Is it moss? Is moss alive? Do you have a family? Do you have a name? What is your name? Is it Gherkin? Why is it Gherkin?"

Gherkin blinked, chewed his lettuce, and then stopped moving entirely. He looked like he was waiting for a bus that would never come.

"Mm," he said.

"That's it? Just Mm?"

"Not yet," Gherkin added, after a pause that felt longer than a math test.

Yusuf was delighted by this. He loved the slow pace and my visible panic. He vibrated in the middle of the Spring Room while I explained the tin's rules to a boy who treated them like suggestions. I made him promise, putting my hand out for a deal. He put his hand in mine, and we performed a spit-shake, which is a handshake where you spit in your palm first. It was gross, but legally binding.

"I will tell no one," Yusuf whispered, his eyes wide and bright.

"Good," I said.

He grinned, his missing teeth catching the sun.
pages.image: A small boy and a thin girl do a spit-shake in a walled garden; an old mossy tortoise watches them from a leafy patch, chewing lettuce, with a rusty tin nearby.

pages.text:
Yusuf kept his secret for exactly four hours, which is impressive for a six-year-old who treats silence like a video game level he is trying to skip.

I found out because Mrs. Ilves stopped me on the stairs, coming down with her knitting bag, the one that always has a ball of wool hanging from it like a pendulum. She looked at me with eyes that had seen everything, including probably the time Yusuf tried to hide a broken plate under the sofa.

"So it's still there," she said, and it was not a question.

My stomach dropped to the floor. "Mrs. Ilves, I can explain."

"You don't have to explain," she said, patting my arm with fingers that were dry and quick as a card trick. "I know. Yusuf told me. Then he told the man at the bakery. Then he told your mother. He is very good at this. Being a boy. He is very good at being a boy."

I felt heat rise up my neck, burning my face until I wanted to sink into the carpet and stay there.

"Yusuf cannot keep a secret," I said, my voice small.

"No," Mrs. Ilves agreed, adjusting her bag. "He cannot. But you can. You have the tape measure. You have the patience. Or you think you do." She smiled, and it was not unkind. "See you in the lift."
pages.image: An elderly woman in a cardigan holds a knitting bag on a concrete stair landing, smiling gently at a thin girl with round glasses who looks shocked and flushed.

pages.text:
Mrs. Ilves lived on the fourth floor, where her window looked out over the car park and she watched everything from it. As she walked past me, she mentioned that the garden used to be the pride of Lowell Court.

"Mr. Osei built it," she said. "With his wife, Ada. They grew food for half the estate. Tomatoes, beans, herbs. The air smelled like summer even in the winter."

I thought of the pear tree, and then the blue flower.

"Then why did it stop?" I asked.

Mrs. Ilves stopped walking and looked at the stained grey wall of the stairwell.

"Ada died," she said. "And Mr. Osei shut the gate. He could not open it. So we stopped talking about it, and we stopped going behind the fence. It was easier that way."

She started walking again, her heels clicking on the concrete.

"Do not tell Mr. Osei I said this," she added. "He is a kind man. He does not need to feel guilty again."

I stood on the landing, my hands shaking behind my back so she would not see.
pages.image: An elderly woman walks down a concrete stairwell, her back to the viewer, while a thin girl with round glasses stands frozen on a landing, holding a notebook tightly.

pages.text:
Mama came home at four. She smelled of soap and tiredness. She did not ask about the garden. She did not ask about Yusuf. She just put her bag down and sat on the edge of my bed.

"You're smiling," she said.

I was. I had been smiling all day. I tried to stop, but it was too late. The smile was already there, stuck to my face like a sticker.

"I'm fine," I said.

"You're not fine," Mama said. "You're smiling when you talk about it. I hadn't seen that in a while."

I looked at her. Her eyes were dark circles, but they were bright. She was looking at me like I was something she had lost and found again. I felt caught. I felt kept.

"I found a garden," I said.

Mama nodded. She did not ask for more. She just sat there, on the edge of my bed, in the quiet room, while the sun went down outside. I lay awake for a long time. I did not check the seed. I did not measure the steps. I just listened to the wind.
pages.image: A tired woman in blue scrubs sits on the edge of a child's bed, smiling softly at a thin girl lying in the dark; a small windowsill plant sits nearby in the dim light.
